scenario_text:
To demonstrate the applicability of LCAnet, we instantiate the ontology network on a real-world LCA study conducted within the SmartACV project called the StorAIge study. This study is aimed at evaluating the environmental impact of a Near Memory Computing prototype based on C-SRAM technology.

The LCA study was conducted using the EIME software tool, connected to a Bill of Materials describing the electronic components of the prototype. Inventory data were sourced from two databases: CODDE (v3.00.000) and NegaOctet. Environmental impact calculations were performed using the Environmental Footprint 3.0 (EF 3.0) methodology. The resulting inventory and impact data, together with study metadata including hypotheses, parametrisation, system boundary, and actor information, were extracted and subsequently used as input data for the use case.

scenario_text: Software reverse engineering is a difficult and tedious process due a lot of the information of the original data (like the names of functions and variables) being lost during the process of disassembly and decompilation. Using reverse engineering software like Ghidra can make this process easier through collecting all the symbols used in a binary file, but these symbols usually don't have their original name (making the process of trying to figure out what they do more difficult). My plan is to make a knowledge graph based on the symbol table in Ghidra to help users more easily visualize how all the data from an executable file fits together. Initially, the knowledge graph will just use the data from the symbol table, with the purpose of it being to more easily see how the data from a binary executable fits together. Especially after a user renames some labels for variables or functions, the knowledge graph would make it easier to visualize how the different pieces work together to gain a better overall understanding of how the program executable works. I also hope to expand the knowledge graph to apply to finding dependency vulnerabilities in a software supply chain. Specifically, connecting malware-specific behavior beyond just one artifact or executable file to detect vulnerabilities within a software supply chain.

What percentage of the functions in the binary file are imported (i.e., external)?

scenario_text: Mike needs to solve a task by prompting a foundation model. Thus, he needs a prompting technique suitable for the task. Moreover, the task involves a specific data modality and is subject to different constraints. Another constraint concerns the model architecture, which depends on the available resources. He may also explore model families, variants, and evolutions in order to experiment with prompts. Furthermore, he relies on the analysis of prior chats to design the solution. Specifically, he can identify which models and prompting techniques are most frequently adopted for different tasks. Regarding usage patterns, he may also be interested in statistics on conversation length and in retrieving responses to specific prompts.

scenario_text: As a representative real-world environment, we take the LyonTech La Doua campus as a navigable environment. A subpart of this campus is illustrated in Figure 1, which contrasts two itineraries connecting points A and B. The shortest route (shown in blue) leaves the starting building directly, follows a tram line and arrives from the west. Another possible route (orange line), which may prove more convenient depending on the user’s preferences, passes through several indoor areas and arrives from the east. Although shorter in distance, the blue itinerary exposes the user to outdoor weather, tramway noise, and a potentially non-accessible entrance, which may pose difficulties to some users. The orange itinerary maximizes indoor traversal, avoids noise, and reaches point B through a more accessible side, which are environmental characteristics that may be looked after by some user. Identifying such an itinerary therefore requires accounting for contextual characteristics as well as user preferences and constraints, including sensory factors (e.g., noise level), physical accessibility (e.g., entrance type, vertical transitions), and dynamic conditions (e.g., weather, lighting). In this section, we describe how we made sure to build an inclusive-by-design ontology. To this end, we collaborated with a domain expert with a background in occupational therapy, who contributed to the elaboration of a reference vocabulary cataloging environmental characteristics considered as potentially relevant to users in pedestrian mobility. Building on this work, we derived several personas, two of which are presented below. The first persona, Anna, is a first-year undergraduate student in Computer Science diagnosed with autism spectrum disorder. She feels uncomfortable in crowded or noisy places and needs opportunities to rest in quiet spaces. Based on Anna’s profile, we derived the following requirements: R1 The routing system should characterize spatial areas through relevant contextual properties (e.g. noise level, crowdedness). R2 The system should identify and help to avoid high-traffic areas during peak hours. R3 The system should be able to locate rest areas along or near to potential routes. The second persona, Sacha, is a master’s student in Sports Science who prefers physically engaging routes (stairs over elevators, outdoor green spaces) and occasionally needs quick access to specific amenities. Her profile motivates the following requirements: R4 The system should distinguish between vertical transition types (stairs, elevators, escalators) to support preference and capability-aware routing. R5 The system should locate the nearest instance of a desired amenity type (vending machine, toilets, reception board) to the current proposed itinerary. R6 The system should characterize spaces based on their aesthetic or comfort-related qualities to enable experience-aware routing.

scenario_text: We used the following running use case to scope the ontology. i. Learner may pursue goals that target skills ii. Learner may have preferences, challenges or awareness over one or more topics or skills iii. Learning objectives are aligned in relation to learner situations and may be supported by pedagogical techniques or learning resource units iv. Assessment exercises use evaluation techniques and metrics to produce results that support feedback (with source and temporal information), awareness observations or learning strategies used. These led to six modeling requirements where APLO needed to represent pedagogical organization, including frameworks, elements and their order; objective alignment across learning objectives, pedagogical techniques and learning resources; evaluation, including assessment exercises, techniques, metrics and results; feedback responses, including source and temporal information; learner context, including goals, preferences, challenges and situations; and learner awareness as topic or skill-scoped information that changes over time.

scenario_text: This example is motivated by a concrete use case from the SMARTY research project, which focuses on scalable and quantum-resilient heterogeneous edge computing enabling trustworthy AI, and includes a specific activity that addresses the semantic management of digital assets (including software) for supporting interoperability. In the context of one of the use cases of the project, a matchmaker is being developed, which addresses the dynamic allocation of hardware resources (DPU and GPU) based on the characteristics and requirements of incoming service requests, by comparing the requirements expressed for a given software with the actual characteristics of software and hardware resources described in a catalogue. The goal of the matchmaker is to identify candidate resources that can be used to execute, support, or deploy the main software.

scenario_text:
Developing stress detection models is inherently complex, including modeling aspects regarding stressors, stress states, physiological responses, sensor measurements, and contextual factors. A stressor (or stimulus) represents an event, condition, or stimulus that has the potential to induce stress in a subject, but whether it does is highly subjective and may depend on the context. Physiological changes, such as decreased heart rate variability, may reflect stress but can also arise from physical activity. Sensor measurements, therefore, provide only indirect cues to stress by capturing physiological or behavioral responses. WISDOM is a structured, machine-readable model for physiology-based stress detection by explicitly linking stressors, stress states, physiological responses, sensors, and contextual information.

In the affective computing domain, specifically within the subdomain of stress detection, model development is mostly restricted to single datasets, while only a few works integrate heterogeneous data sources. Datasets often differ in terms of sensor, experimental protocol, demographics, and other factors. To this extent, previous research proposes standardization of experiments and data collection for affective computing, specifically stress datasets [23], aiming to structure stress research experiments. However, in general, stress detection research and data collection lack a unified semantic structure, as shown by the diverse experimental protocols in this domain (e.g., [2, 24, 25, 6]). The WISDOM ontology addresses this challenge by providing a formalized and extensible conceptual data model for representing stress conditions, as well as sensor- and wearable-device-related data structures.

The WISDOM ontology offers a wide range of potential application scenarios across different areas of stress research. By providing a formal and semantically rich representation of stress conditions, related activities, and physiological signals, the ontology supports tasks that rely on structured, interoperable, and machine-readable stress detection:

Semantic annotation of wearable stress datasets. WISDOM-Stress can annotate physiological records with information about subject, sensor, signal channel, observable property, activity phase, and stress condition. For example, an electrodermal activity (EDA) signal channel can be linked to electrodermal activity, an EDA sensor, a subject, and a cognitive stress phase. Thus, it can be systematically compared to an EDA signal from the same dataset or across other heterogeneous datasets. For instance, this assessment may be used to compare general signal quality or EDA response to semantically different stress stimuli.

Dataset harmonization and comparison. Different datasets may use different labels, such as baseline, stress, cognitive task, social stress, relaxation, or recovery. The ontology can help map these labels into a shared semantic structure. In this way, WISDOM supports a unified terminology across different datasets, thus enhancing the comparability of physiological signals during the presence or absence of stress stimuli. Importantly, WISDOM does not require the original dataset taxonomies to be identical or to be replaced. Instead, dataset-specific labels can be aligned with the more general semantic concepts represented in WISDOM while preserving their original meaning and provenance. For example, two datasets may classify the same experimental task differently, such as ”stress” in one dataset and ”cognitive workload” in another. Rather than treating these labels as automatically equivalent, WISDOM allows the underlying activity, associated stressor, and stress condition to be represented separately. This enables semantically compatible aspects of heterogeneous taxonomies to be aligned while retaining distinctions where the original classifications differ. Where labels cannot be mapped unambiguously, the ontology does not resolve the conflict automatically; such mappings require dataset-specific interpretation and, where necessary, manual expert alignment.

Contextual interpretation of physiological observations. The ontology can represent that an elevated heart rate occurred during a physical stress phase, not necessarily a cognitive or socio-evaluative stressor. This is crucial because sensor values alone are not sufficient for stress interpretation.

Digital Twins and Condition Simulations. The ontology provides a structural backbone for building physiological digital twins by modeling different types of conditions and an individual’s physiological responses [26]. Publicly available datasets in the domain of stress recognition are sparse, typically characterized by few subjects (e.g., [2, 27]), as well as heterogeneous study protocols. Approaches that treat all stress conditions the same might fail to distinguish between different stress stimuli, such as the socio-evaluative stress and cognitive stress types elicited through the Trier Social Stress Test (TSST) [28]. In this regard, data integration through a semantically rich stress ontology that bridges psychological concepts of stress and wearable sensor-based stress experiments facilitates analysis and simulation of physiological responses to stress stimuli, recovery phases, or absence of stress.
